# Problem 1

## (a) Download and merge the datasets
```{r}
library(haven)

aux <- read_xpt("data/AUX_I.xpt")
demo <- read_xpt("data/DEMO_I.xpt")

nhanes <- merge(aux, demo, by = "SEQN")

dim(nhanes)
```

\

## (b) Data cleaning

```{r}
nhanes$RIAGENDR <- factor(
  nhanes$RIAGENDR,
  levels = c(1, 2),
  labels = c("Male", "Female")
)

```

```{r}
nhanes$DMDCITZN[nhanes$DMDCITZN %in% c(7, 9)] <- NA

nhanes$DMDCITZN <- factor(
  nhanes$DMDCITZN,
  levels = c(1, 2),
  labels = c("Citizen", "Not a citizen")
)

```

```{r}
nhanes$INDHHIN2[nhanes$INDHHIN2 %in% c(77, 99)] <- NA

nhanes$INDHHIN2 <- factor(
  nhanes$INDHHIN2,
  levels = c(1:10, 14, 15, 13, 12),
  labels = c(
    "$0-$4,999",
    "$5,000-$9,999",
    "$10,000-$14,999",
    "$15,000-$19,999",
    "$20,000-$24,999",
    "$25,000-$34,999",
    "$35,000-$44,999",
    "$45,000-$54,999",
    "$55,000-$64,999",
    "$65,000-$74,999",
    "$75,000-$99,999",
    "$100,000 and over",
    "Under $20,000 (broad)",
    "$20,000 and over (broad)"
  )
)

```

The original income codes do not follow a strictly increasing income order. I rearranged the detailed income categories from lowest to highest and placed the two broad, overlapping categories separately at the end, as they cannot be precisely ordered among the detailed income categories.

\

## (c) Poisson regression models

```{r}
nhanes$income_numeric <- as.numeric(nhanes$INDHHIN2)

nhanes$income_numeric[nhanes$income_numeric > 12] <- NA

```

```{r}
model_1r <- glm(
  AUXTWIDR ~ RIAGENDR,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

```

```{r}
model_2r <- glm(
  AUXTWIDR ~ RIAGENDR + DMDCITZN + DMDHHSZA + income_numeric,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

```

```{r}
model_1l <- glm(
  AUXTWIDL ~ RIAGENDR,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

```

```{r}
model_2l <- glm(
  AUXTWIDL ~ RIAGENDR + DMDCITZN + DMDHHSZA + income_numeric,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

```

```{r}
irr_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c(
    "Intercept (exp(coefficient))",
    "Female",
    "Not a citizen",
    "Children (per unit)",
    "Income level (per unit)"
  ),
  `1R` = c(exp(coef(model_1r)), rep(NA_real_, 3)),
  `2R` = exp(coef(model_2r)),
  `1L` = c(exp(coef(model_1l)), rep(NA_real_, 3)),
  `2L` = exp(coef(model_2l)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

options(knitr.kable.NA = "-")
```


```{r}
knitr::kable(
  irr_table,
  row.names = FALSE,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Exponentiated coefficients from the four Poisson regression models"
)

```

\

```{r}
model_stats <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Sample size", "Pseudo-R2 (deviance-based)", "AIC"),
  `1R` = c(
    format(nobs(model_1r), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.6f", 1 - deviance(model_1r) / model_1r$null.deviance),
    format(round(AIC(model_1r)), big.mark = ",")
  ),
  `2R` = c(
    format(nobs(model_2r), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.6f", 1 - deviance(model_2r) / model_2r$null.deviance),
    format(round(AIC(model_2r)), big.mark = ",")
  ),
  `1L` = c(
    format(nobs(model_1l), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.6f", 1 - deviance(model_1l) / model_1l$null.deviance),
    format(round(AIC(model_1l)), big.mark = ",")
  ),
  `2L` = c(
    format(nobs(model_2l), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%.6f", 1 - deviance(model_2l) / model_2l$null.deviance),
    format(round(AIC(model_2l)), big.mark = ",")
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  model_stats,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Model statistics for the four Poisson regression models"
)

```

\

## (d) Hypothesis tests

```{r}
gender_test <- coef(summary(model_2l))["RIAGENDRFemale", ]

gender_test

exp(coef(model_2l)["RIAGENDRFemale"])
```

```{r}
emm_gender <- emmeans::emmeans(
  model_2l,
  ~ RIAGENDR
)

summary(emm_gender, type = "response")

```

```{r}
gender_diff <- pairs(
  emmeans::regrid(emm_gender, transform = "response"),
  reverse = TRUE
)

summary(gender_diff, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE))

```

### Test 1 — IRR Comparison

For Model 2L, the estimated female-to-male IRR is 1.0187. The Wald test gives $z = 5.160$ and $p = 2.47 \times 10^{-7}$. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis that the IRR equals 1 at the 5% significance level. Holding other covariates constant, females have approximately 1.87% higher expected left-ear tympanometric width than males.

### Test 2 — Predicted Value Comparison

The adjusted predicted values are 84.8 for males and 86.3 for females. The estimated difference (Female − Male) is 1.59, with a 95% confidence interval of $[0.986, 2.19]$. The test gives $z = 5.161$ and $p < 0.0001$. Since the confidence interval excludes 0, we reject the null hypothesis of equal predicted values at the 5% significance level.

### Note on Overdispersion

These results are based on the standard Poisson model. Since the model shows evidence of overdispersion, the reported p-values and confidence intervals should be interpreted cautiously.

# Problem 2 - Sakila

```{r}
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(
  RSQLite::SQLite(),
  "data/sakila_master.db"
)

```

## (a) Customers and active percentages by store

### Method 1 - SQL + R

```{r}
customer_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT store_id, active FROM customer"
)

customer_counts <- table(customer_data$store_id)

active_percent <- tapply(
  customer_data$active == "1",
  customer_data$store_id,
  mean
) * 100

result_r <- data.frame(
  store_id = as.integer(names(customer_counts)),
  customers = as.integer(customer_counts),
  percent_active = as.numeric(active_percent)
)

knitr::kable(
  result_r,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Customer counts and active percentages by store (SQL + R)"
)

```

### Method 2 - Single SQL Query

```{r}
result_sql <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT
     store_id,
     COUNT(*) AS customers,
     ROUND(
       100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN active = '1' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*),
       2
     ) AS percent_active
   FROM customer
   GROUP BY store_id
   ORDER BY store_id"
)

knitr::kable(
  result_sql,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Customer counts and active percentages by store (SQL only)"
)

```

### Performance comparison

```{r}
bench_a <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  SQL_R = {
    data_r <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT store_id, active FROM customer"
    )

    counts_r <- table(data_r$store_id)

    percent_r <- tapply(
      data_r$active == "1",
      data_r$store_id,
      mean
    ) * 100

    data.frame(
      store_id = as.integer(names(counts_r)),
      customers = as.integer(counts_r),
      percent_active = as.numeric(percent_r)
    )
  },
  SQL_only = {
    dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT
         store_id,
         COUNT(*) AS customers,
         ROUND(
           100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN active = '1' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*),
           2
         ) AS percent_active
       FROM customer
       GROUP BY store_id
       ORDER BY store_id"
    )
  },
  times = 100L
)

bench_summary <- summary(bench_a, unit = "us")

median_sql_r <- bench_summary$median[bench_summary$expr == "SQL_R"]
median_sql_only <- bench_summary$median[bench_summary$expr == "SQL_only"]

bench_summary

```

The microbenchmark results show that the SQL-only approach is faster than the SQL + R approach. Over 100 evaluations, the median execution times were approximately `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_only)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_r)` microseconds, respectively. Thus, the SQL-only approach was about `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_r / median_sql_only)` times faster in this benchmark, likely because the aggregation was performed directly in the database.

\

## (b) Staff names and countries

### Method 1 - SQL + R

```{r}
staff_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT staff_id, first_name, last_name, address_id FROM staff"
)

address_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT address_id, city_id FROM address"
)

city_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT city_id, country_id FROM city"
)

country_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT country_id, country FROM country"
)

staff_info <- merge(staff_data, address_data, by = "address_id")
staff_info <- merge(staff_info, city_data, by = "city_id")
staff_info <- merge(staff_info, country_data, by = "country_id")

result_r_b <- data.frame(
  staff_id = staff_info$staff_id,
  staff_name = paste(staff_info$first_name, staff_info$last_name),
  country = staff_info$country
)

result_r_b <- result_r_b[order(result_r_b$staff_id), ]

knitr::kable(
  result_r_b,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Staff names and countries (SQL + R)"
)

```

\

### Method 2 - Single SQL Query

```{r}
result_sql_b <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT
     s.staff_id,
     s.first_name || ' ' || s.last_name AS staff_name,
     co.country
   FROM staff AS s
   JOIN address AS a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
   JOIN city AS ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
   JOIN country AS co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
   ORDER BY s.staff_id"
)

knitr::kable(
  result_sql_b,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Staff names and countries (SQL only)"
)

```

### Performance comparison

```{r}
bench_b <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  SQL_R = {
    staff_b <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT staff_id, first_name, last_name, address_id FROM staff"
    )

    address_b <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT address_id, city_id FROM address"
    )

    city_b <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT city_id, country_id FROM city"
    )

    country_b <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT country_id, country FROM country"
    )

    info_b <- merge(staff_b, address_b, by = "address_id")
    info_b <- merge(info_b, city_b, by = "city_id")
    info_b <- merge(info_b, country_b, by = "country_id")

    result_b <- data.frame(
      staff_id = info_b$staff_id,
      staff_name = paste(info_b$first_name, info_b$last_name),
      country = info_b$country
    )

    result_b[order(result_b$staff_id), ]
  },
  SQL_only = {
    dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT
         s.staff_id,
         s.first_name || ' ' || s.last_name AS staff_name,
         co.country
       FROM staff AS s
       JOIN address AS a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
       JOIN city AS ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
       JOIN country AS co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
       ORDER BY s.staff_id"
    )
  },
  times = 100L
)

bench_summary_b <- summary(bench_b, unit = "us")

median_sql_r_b <- bench_summary_b$median[bench_summary_b$expr == "SQL_R"]
median_sql_only_b <- bench_summary_b$median[bench_summary_b$expr == "SQL_only"]

bench_summary_b

```

The microbenchmark results show that the SQL-only approach is faster than the SQL + R approach. Over 100 evaluations, the median execution times were approximately `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_only_b)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_r_b)` microseconds, respectively. Thus, the SQL-only approach was about `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_r_b / median_sql_only_b)` times faster in this benchmark, likely because it performs the joins directly in the database, avoiding multiple data transfers and additional merging operations in R.

## (c) Films rented for the highest dollar value

### Method 1 - SQL + R

```{r}
payment_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT rental_id, amount FROM payment"
)

rental_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT rental_id, inventory_id FROM rental"
)

inventory_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT inventory_id, film_id FROM inventory"
)

film_data <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT film_id, title FROM film"
)

film_payments <- merge(payment_data, rental_data, by = "rental_id")
film_payments <- merge(film_payments, inventory_data, by = "inventory_id")
film_payments <- merge(film_payments, film_data, by = "film_id")

max_amount <- max(film_payments$amount)

result_r_c <- unique(
  film_payments[film_payments$amount == max_amount, c("title", "amount")]
)

result_r_c <- result_r_c[order(result_r_c$title), ]

names(result_r_c) <- c("film_title", "payment_usd")
rownames(result_r_c) <- NULL

knitr::kable(
  result_r_c,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Films rented for the highest dollar value (SQL + R)"
)

```

\

### Method 2 - Single SQL Query

```{r}
result_sql_c <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT DISTINCT
     f.title AS film_title,
     p.amount AS payment_usd
   FROM payment AS p
   JOIN rental AS r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
   JOIN inventory AS i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
   JOIN film AS f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
   WHERE p.amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM payment)
   ORDER BY f.title"
)

knitr::kable(
  result_sql_c,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Films rented for the highest dollar value (SQL only)"
)

```

\

### Performance comparison

```{r}
bench_c <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  SQL_R = {
    payment_c <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT rental_id, amount FROM payment"
    )

    rental_c <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT rental_id, inventory_id FROM rental"
    )

    inventory_c <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT inventory_id, film_id FROM inventory"
    )

    film_c <- dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT film_id, title FROM film"
    )

    film_payments_c <- merge(payment_c, rental_c, by = "rental_id")
    film_payments_c <- merge(film_payments_c, inventory_c, by = "inventory_id")
    film_payments_c <- merge(film_payments_c, film_c, by = "film_id")

    max_amount_c <- max(film_payments_c$amount)

    result_c <- unique(
      film_payments_c[film_payments_c$amount == max_amount_c, c("title", "amount")]
    )

    result_c <- result_c[order(result_c$title), ]

    names(result_c) <- c("film_title", "payment_usd")
    rownames(result_c) <- NULL

    result_c
  },
  SQL_only = {
    dbGetQuery(
      con,
      "SELECT DISTINCT
         f.title AS film_title,
         p.amount AS payment_usd
       FROM payment AS p
       JOIN rental AS r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
       JOIN inventory AS i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
       JOIN film AS f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
       WHERE p.amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM payment)
       ORDER BY f.title"
    )
  },
  times = 100L
)

bench_summary_c <- summary(bench_c, unit = "us")

median_sql_r_c <- bench_summary_c$median[bench_summary_c$expr == "SQL_R"]
median_sql_only_c <- bench_summary_c$median[bench_summary_c$expr == "SQL_only"]

bench_summary_c

```

The microbenchmark results show that the SQL-only approach is faster than the SQL + R approach. Over 100 evaluations, the median execution times were approximately `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_only_c)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_r_c)` microseconds, respectively. Thus, the SQL-only approach was about `r sprintf("%.2f", median_sql_r_c / median_sql_only_c)` times faster in this benchmark, likely because it performs the joins and filtering directly in the database, reducing data transfer and additional processing in R.
